summary: Introductory hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, core parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retry/backoff strategies, and console visibility. SE demoed a small live sandbox call; discussion covered latency vs cost tradeoffs, prefix/KV caching, and security/compliance questions (SOC2, SSO, KMS). Agreed next steps: pricing, perf benchmarks on customer data, and pilot kickoff.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-20 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood Product), Carlos (BrightBridge CTO), Priya (Lead ML Eng), Asha (PM), Ethan (SRE)

[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Liam who will do most of the technical demo. Quick roundtable - can you confirm folks on the BrightBridge side?
[00:00:08] Carlos: Yep, Carlos here. CTO. Priya, Asha, Ethan all on.
[00:00:12] Priya: Hi, Priya.
[00:00:13] Asha: Asha here.
[00:00:14] Ethan: Ethan, SRE.
[00:00:16] Maya: Great. Goal for today is to show the hosted conversational API basics — streaming, params, and how to handle retries — and give a peek at the console/optimize signals. We'll keep it interactive. Liam?
[00:00:27] Liam: Thanks. I'll start with a short slide, then we'll do a live sandbox call against the hosted endpoint so you can see streaming. Then we'll talk about parameters — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop tokens — and retry patterns.
[00:00:40] Liam: One quick note: our docs sometimes call it "conversations" API or "chatgen" in internal docs, so you might see slightly different names.
[00:00:48] Carlos: Fine. We're mainly evaluating for customer support automation, so latency matters. Also security: we need to know about encryption and audit logs.
[00:00:56] Maya: Noted. We'll hit security later.
[00:00:58] Liam: Ok jumping in — here's a simple HTTP request to the hosted generations endpoint. (screen share) You send a JSON payload with messages, model, and the stream flag to true to get partial token stream.
[00:01:15] [00:01:15] Liam: Starting a live call now — you'll see chunks come in as the model generates.
[00:01:18] [00:01:18] Speaker 1 (sandbox): [partial] "Sure — to process the refund, could you provide the order ID..."
[00:01:22] Priya: I can see the partial tokens. Is it SSE or websockets?
[00:01:25] Liam: We support SSE-style streaming over the same HTTPS request; it behaves like server-sent events. For web clients you can also use our SDKs which wrap that.
[00:01:32] Asha: How frequent are partial events?
[00:01:34] Liam: It depends on generation speed and chunking. Typically you get updates every 50-150ms of token production, but if there are latency spikes they may batch. You can configure the truncation/flush size in advanced settings.
[00:01:45] Ethan: If a stream connection drops mid-generation, what's best practice?
[00:01:48] Liam: Good question. Two patterns: 1) Client reconnect & resume — our SDKs provide a token-cursor so you can resume from last confirmed token in some cases; 2) Retry the full request with idempotency key and let the runtime detect overlap and return from cache if prefix caching is available. For long-running chats we recommend prefix/KV caching to avoid re-computation.
[00:02:04] Priya: Prefix caching — do you do any automatic caching or is it per-customer config?
[00:02:07] Liam: It's workload-aware. Hosted defaults include lightweight prefix caching for repeated system prompts and high-hit prefixes. For customer-specific caching and eviction policies you can configure via the console or Dedicated private configs.
[00:02:18] [00:02:18] Speaker 1 (sandbox): [partial] "...and we'll process that right away. Also, could you confirm whether you'd like a refund or store credit?"
[00:02:23] Carlos: On cost — how does streaming affect billing vs non-streaming?
[00:02:27] Maya: We bill per token generated and per embedding units when applicable. Streaming doesn't change token billing; it's just the transport. However, network usage is slightly higher due to SSE framing but not materially. The big cost levers are model choice, max_tokens and batching.
[00:02:41] Liam: Right, and batching can dramatically reduce per-token costs when you have many short requests. Our Optimize tool will suggest batch sizes and quantization if you run an evaluation trace.
[00:02:51] Asha: Can you show examples of param tuning for determinism? We're concerned about consistent replies for transactional messages.
[00:02:58] Liam: Sure. Lower temperature (0.0-0.2) and narrower top_p (e.g., 0.7) make outputs deterministic. Also pin a model version; we provide versioned artifacts so same model+params reproduce results. If you absolutely need deterministic mapping, you can use a reranking stage or a template-based fallback.
[00:03:13] Priya: Do you recommend temperature 0 for refunds?
[00:03:17] Liam: For transactional flows yes, temperature 0 and defined stop tokens works well. For creative copy you can bump to 0.8.
[00:03:22] [00:03:22] Speaker 1 (sandbox): "Refund processed. Would you prefer store credit or a full refund?"
[00:03:25] Carlos: About retries — what's Redwood's typical retry/backoff guidance? We have to handle transient 502s at our edge.
[00:03:31] Liam: We recommend exponential backoff with jitter and an idempotency key per user-turn. The runtime returns clear error codes; for 429/overload we suggest a 500-2000ms base backoff, doubling with cap around 10s. For network resets try immediate small retry once and then backoff.
[00:03:45] Maya: We also have client SDKs with built-in retry logic that capture best practices so teams don't have to implement from scratch.
[00:03:49] Ethan: Any SLA or rate limits we should expect on hosted?
[00:03:52] Maya: Hosted has soft rate limits per API key; for production we recommend Dedicated or committed capacity if you need predictable throughput and SLA-backed latency. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and autoscaling policies.
[00:04:04] Asha: If we start hosted and then need to move to Dedicated later, is that a big migration?
[00:04:08] Maya: It's designed to be seamless — same API surface, same model versions. You just update routing policy in the console and can pin versions. We can run a canary migration with automatic fallback as well.
[00:04:16] Liam: I'll switch to the console — quick tour of traces and cost breakdown per route. (screen share) Here you can see token-level cost, median latency, and a timeline of retries and failures per API key.
[00:04:30] [00:04:30] Speaker 1 (console): [UI narration] "Token usage: 1.2M/mo, median latency 230ms"
[00:04:35] Priya: That latency number — is that warm or cold?
[00:04:37] Liam: It's end-to-end median for the observed time window; we provide cold-start percentiles separately. If you care about 99p latency we can surface that too.
[00:04:44] Carlos: Security — can you confirm SOC 2 and KMS integrations? We need SSO via SAML and customer-managed keys.
[00:04:51] Maya: Yes — hosted is SOC 2 compliant (Type II), we support SAML/SCIM for SSO and RBAC, and for Private deployments we offer KMS/HSM integrations for customer key control. For hosted we also have envelope encryption options and audit logs per request. I'll share the security pack after the call.
[00:05:05] Priya: Are audit logs full transcript or only metadata?
[00:05:08] Maya: We can configure retention policy: metadata-only or full transcripts; for PCI/PHI workloads we recommend Private deployment and retention minimized.
[00:05:16] Asha: Can you show an example of a retry header or idempotency key in the request?
[00:05:20] Liam: Sure — in the example I'll include an Idempotency-Key header with the user-turn UUID. If you send the same key our runtime deduplicates and can serve cached response if identical prefix was processed.
[00:05:30] [00:05:30] Speaker 1 (sandbox): [partial] "Idempotency key received, checking cache..."
[00:05:33] Priya: For throughput testing — can you run a quick synthetic with 128-token median and batching 8?
[00:05:39] Liam: We can, but I need 5-10 minutes to kick a small perf job. If you want, I can run a short 60s demo now with low concurrency to show behavior.
[00:05:47] Carlos: Go ahead.
[00:05:48] Liam: Kicking off a small load — 20 concurrent requests, batch size 4, model = rdx-medium (example). Watch the console metrics.
[00:05:58] [00:05:58] Speaker 1 (console): "Throughput spike detected, batching efficiency +23%"
[00:06:02] Ethan: We're seeing queuing — what's the queue threshold triggers?
[00:06:05] Liam: The runtime uses a latency budget per-request. If queue backlog grows past the threshold, requests either wait up to a short cap or are overflowed to a capacity-tier fallback depending on your routing policy. You can configure burst limits and fallback to cheaper model variants to preserve availability.
[00:06:18] Maya: Quick Q from our side — are you sensitive to model size (e.g., 7B vs 70B) for cost?
[00:06:23] Carlos: Yes, cost matters. We want sub-300ms median for text generation for live chat.
[00:06:28] Liam: For sub-300ms median, a 13B or 7B optimized quantized profile on a low-latency instance usually fits, depending on tokens. We can run a benchmark with your prompt shapes to recommend model+quantization. That's part of the Optimize playbook.
[00:06:40] Priya: About model variants — do you have fallback chains? For example degrade to cheaper model when overloaded?
[00:06:44] Liam: Yes — routing policies allow primary model + fallback list. You can also specify cost vs latency priorities so the runtime picks a policy at request-time.
[00:06:52] [00:06:52] Speaker 1 (sandbox): [partial] "Fallback to rdx-small initiated..."
[00:06:55] Asha: Helpful. Any built-in synthesis or reranking to keep quality consistent when falling back?
[00:07:00] Liam: We recommend a small reranker step or confidence thresholds. Optimize can surface quality regressions if fallback models produce lower BLEU/ROUGE or semantic similarity on your eval sets.
[00:07:11] Maya: Back to streaming — some browsers choke on long SSE streams. Any known pitfalls?
[00:07:15] Liam: Long-lived SSE clients can accumulate memory; we recommend chunked consumers and incremental flush. The SDKs stream to a readable stream so the app can handle partial outputs and release memory.
[00:07:25] Priya: In the live demo, are we using the JS SDK?
[00:07:27] Liam: Yes, small Node snippet. I'll paste it to the chat. (pastes snippet)
[00:07:33] [00:07:33] Liam: Example: const stream = client.chat.stream({model: 'rdx-medium', messages, stream: true}); stream.on('data', chunk => { appendToUI(chunk.text) });
[00:07:45] Carlos: Anything we need to instrument on our side for tracing requests through our stack?
[00:07:49] Ethan: We use distributed tracing; do you propagate trace IDs?
[00:07:51] Liam: We accept and echo back trace headers; you can correlate logs with the request id. Console also shows per-request trace links.
[00:07:58] Asha: If we hit hallucinations, what's the recommended pattern?
[00:08:02] Liam: For hallucinations: 1) constrain with system prompt and stronger grounding, 2) use retrieval augmented generation (RAG) with KVs/doc retriever, 3) apply deterministic params and optionally a post-hoc verifier or API-based fact-checker.
[00:08:13] Priya: Is there a built-in retriever or do we plug our own?
[00:08:16] Liam: We have a built-in retriever connector for popular stores and you can also bring your own via API.
[00:08:21] [00:08:21] Speaker 1 (sandbox): "Response complete. Final: 'Refund processed. Store credit or full refund?'"
[00:08:27] Carlos: That was pretty quick.
[00:08:29] Liam: Yeah that's a short prompt. For longer contexts, KV cache helps with long chats so you don't re-run the whole context each time.
[00:08:36] Priya: Any gotchas with token counting — do system messages count?
[00:08:39] Liam: Yes, all messages included in the request count toward the total token usage. System and user messages, plus completion tokens. We surface token breakdown in the response headers for visibility.
[00:08:49] Maya: We are around the 25-minute mark — wanted to surface commercial packaging quickly: hosted usage pricing vs Dedicated reserved capacity. If you're starting small, hosted is easiest; if you need guaranteed throughput, Dedicated reserved commits lower unit costs.
[00:09:02] Carlos: Could you email a rough cost model for 1M tokens/month with the recommended model?
[00:09:06] Maya: Yep, will include that in the pricing email.
[00:09:09] Ethan: For security again, if we use hosted but want customer-managed keys, is that possible?
[00:09:14] Maya: For hosted we support envelope encryption with customer KMS in some regions; full KMS/HSM control is available on Private. We'll include specifics in the security pack.
[00:09:23] [00:09:23] Speaker 1 (console): "Audit log: request id x1234 by api-key-abcd"
[00:09:26] Priya: On SDKs — do you have a Python streaming client?
[00:09:29] Liam: Yes, Python, Node, and Go SDKs all support streaming and automatic retries. I'll link the repos.
[00:09:35] Asha: Can we do a short role-play where we call the API from our web client with failure simulation?
[00:09:39] Liam: Sure — simulate a 502 at the edge and show retry flow. (runs a failure sim)
[00:09:45] [00:09:45] Speaker 1 (sandbox): "Error 502 - upstream"
[00:09:47] Liam: Our client retries once quickly, logs the error, then applies exponential backoff. You can toggle behaviour in the client config.
[00:09:53] Priya: If we get partial output and then 502, is there a safe way to resume?
[00:09:57] Liam: If partial tokens were acknowledged, use the cursor to resume. If not, best to retry with idempotency and let cache handle duplication. There's some nuance for multi-turn where you may need server-side state or KV to avoid duplication.
[00:10:10] Carlos: Ok this is helpful. Any notes about latency under load?
[00:10:13] Liam: Generally with batching you trade per-token cost for slightly higher latency for individual requests. For chat with strict latency you set small batch windows and prefer lower-latency model profiles. Optimize will recommend configurations based on your traffic shape.
[00:10:25] Maya: Quick reminder — we'll share a recorded console tour and a cheat sheet for streaming parameters.
[00:10:31] [00:10:31] Speaker 1 (sandbox): "New tokens: 'We have processed the refund'"
[00:10:35] Asha: One last quick question — how do you do version rollouts? We want to A/B different prompts or model params.
[00:10:40] Liam: We support canary rollouts and A/B routing at the config layer. You can route X% to variant B and collect metrics. Console shows per-route metrics so you can measure latency, cost, and quality regressions.
[00:10:52] Priya: Do we get diffs for prompt-based regressions?
[00:10:55] Liam: Optimize includes evals tied to prompt sets so you can detect regressions and surface examples.
[00:11:01] Maya: We're at about 40 minutes — open to any final deep questions.
[00:11:06] Carlos: One more on privacy: do you store data from hosted by default?
[00:11:10] Maya: Hosted stores request logs for a default retention window for debugging; you can change retention or opt for metadata-only. For regulated data we recommend Private deployments.
[00:11:20] Priya: For pilot — we will want a 2-week pilot with a small dataset and perf targets.
[00:11:24] Maya: Sounds good. We'll propose a pilot scope in the pricing email.
[00:11:28] Asha: Can you include the list of required stakeholders from your side for the pilot?
[00:11:32] Maya: Sure — AE, SE, Solutions Eng, and a dedicated onboarding engineer.
[00:11:36] Liam: I'll follow up on the perf tests.
[00:11:38] [00:11:38] Speaker 1 (sandbox): "Session closed."
[00:11:40] Maya: Quick recap: Maya to send pricing and security pack; Liam to run perf benchmarks on customer prompts; Priya to send prompt templates/traffic profile. Proposed pilot kickoff week of 2025-06-30. Any questions?
[00:11:55] Carlos: No, thanks. Useful session.
[00:11:58] Priya: Thanks all.
[00:11:59] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll get notes and next steps over.

[END TRANSCRIPT]

Notes on transcription quality: medium — occasional mis-attribution, some filler words removed, product names sometimes abbreviated. References shared during call: console tour recording (link in follow-up), security pack PDF (link), pricing spreadsheet (link).
